(In this context, a three-term arithmetic progression is a triple of the form (a; ad; ad2) with a; d 2 G; d 6= 1.) For nite abelian groups G known upper and lower bounds for r3(G) are appallingly far apart. Can one exhibit an in nite family of nite non-abelian groups G and give lower and upper bounds for r3(G) which are within a constant factor? Does there exist an in nite family of non-abelian groups G for which r3(G) > jGj= logK jGj, with an absolute constant K? Gowers considers in several related problems, and in particular the following one. Fix 2 (0; 1]. Do there exist in nitely many primes p such that if G = PSL2(p) (see Problem 3.3 for the de nition) and A; B; C G satisfy minfjAj; jBj; jCjg > jGj, then A B C contains a triple (a; da; d2a) with a; d 2 G? Note that the similar property fails for abelian groups with a \large" cyclic component, at least for small ; for example, if N is a positive integer, A = B = (0; N=4) Z=N Z, and C = (N=2; 3N=4) Z=N Z, then A B C does not contain any triple of the form (a; a+d; a+2d) with a; d 2 Z=N Z. Letting b = da and c = d2a one sees that Gowers's question is equivalent to asking whether there is a solution to c = ba 1b with (a; b; c) 2 A B C. Replacing A with the set of its inverses, one can further restate the question to seek triples (a; b; c) 2 A B C with c = bab. It is worth noting that writing arithmetic progressions as (a; da; d2a) (as in Gower's paper) is equivalent to writing them as (a; ad; ad2); indeed, writing = a 1da we nd that (a; da; d2a) = (a; a ; a 2). Two further questions in the spirit of Gowers's problem are the following. Given K > 0, do there exist in nitely many groups G such that for any subset A G with jAj jGj= logK jGj there are a; b; c 2 A, satisfying c = ba 1b? Do there exist in nitely many groups G and subsets A G with jAj > jGj= logK jGj for which there are no such a; b; c 2 A? This second question is equivalent to the question above of whether r3(G) > jGj= logK jGj.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For a finite group $G$, define a three-term arithmetic progression in $G$ to be a triple of the form $(a,\,ad,\,ad^2)$ with $a,d\in G$ and $d\neq 1$. Let $r_3(G)$ denote the largest cardinality of a subset $S\subseteq G$ that contains no three-term arithmetic progression. Address the following questions.

(a) Exhibit an infinite family $\{G_n\}_{n\ge1}$ of finite non-abelian groups together with explicit functions $f(G_n)\le r_3(G_n)\le F(G_n)$ such that $F(G_n)/f(G_n)$ is bounded above by an absolute constant independent of $n$.

(b) Determine whether there exists an absolute constant $K>0$ and an infinite family of finite non-abelian groups $\{G_n\}$ with $|G_n|\to\infty$ such that
$$r_3(G_n) \;>\; \frac{|G_n|}{(\log |G_n|)^K}.$$

(c) (Gowers-type question.) Fix $\theta\in(0,1]$. Decide whether there exist infinitely many primes $p$ such that, taking $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{F}_p)$, for every triple of subsets $A,B,C\subseteq G$ satisfying $\min\{|A|,|B|,|C|\}>\theta|G|$ the Cartesian product $A\times B\times C$ contains a triple of the form $(a,\,da,\,d^2a)$ for some $a,d\in G$. (Equivalently, asking whether there exist $a\in A$, $b\in B$, $c\in C$ with $c=ba^{-1}b$.)

(d) Given $K>0$, decide whether there exist infinitely many finite groups $G$ such that every subset $A\subseteq G$ with $|A|\ge|G|/(\log|G|)^K$ contains elements $a,b,c\in A$ satisfying $c=ba^{-1}b$; and decide whether there exist infinitely many finite groups $G$ admitting subsets $A\subseteq G$ with $|A|>|G|/(\log|G|)^K$ in which no such triple $(a,b,c)$ exists.
artifact.status_search_result: The mixing/Gowers-style question in part (c) for $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(p)$ and related quasirandom or finite simple groups has been resolved: results of Tao (for $\mathrm{SL}_d(\mathbb{F}_q)$) and Peluse (for all non-abelian finite simple groups), together with subsequent work on mixing of three-term progressions in quasirandom groups, establish the desired mixing for triples $(x,xg,xg^2)$. However, the quantitative questions on $r_3(G)$ for infinite families of non-abelian groups (parts (a), (b), and the log-power versions in (d)) do not appear to have been settled in the literature found, so the overall problem is best classified as partially solved.

status_evidence.title: Mixing for progressions in non-abelian groups
status_evidence.snippet: For length three progressions (x,xg,xg^2), we obtain a strong mixing property with polynomial error term in SL_d(F), answering a question of Gowers for this class of groups.
status_evidence.claim: Gowers's mixing question for three-term progressions is resolved for SL_d(F) by Tao.

status_evidence.title: Mixing of 3-Term Progressions in Quasirandom Groups
status_evidence.snippet: We show the mixing of three-term progressions (x, xg, xg^2) in every finite quasirandom group, fully answering a question of Gowers.
status_evidence.claim: The Gowers mixing question for 3-term progressions has been answered for all finite quasirandom groups.

status_evidence.title: Mixing for progressions in nonabelian groups (Forum of Math, Sigma)
status_evidence.snippet: Mixing for progressions in non-abelian groups, extending to non-abelian finite simple groups.
status_evidence.claim: Peluse extended the mixing result to all non-abelian finite simple groups, covering PSL_2(p).
